blocks.text: The locust is a wandering and unsteady animal, which is driven hither and thither at the slightest impulse and is carried anywhere with an easy leap or flight. Hence Iob. XXXIX, 20. (var. 23.) says of the horse, Have you made him move like a locust? that is, leap with equal agility. So in the Chaldee paraphrast on Ierem. LI, 27. Let their horses come up מסככין הא כוחלא, leaping like locusts. Accordingly, just as in Hebrew חרגל chargol is a kind of locust, so in Arabic حرجل [ḥarjal] chargala is said of a horse that عدا يمينة أو يسرة [ʿadā yamīnatan aw yasratan], leaps to the right or to the left ^{(8)}, a verb plainly made from the leap of the locust, as was noted in its place ^{a)}. And David says of himself, Psal. CIX, 23. I am shaken off like a locust, which, when it lacks a nest, wanders and is carried from hedge to hedge. For David is thought to have written this Psalm when, fleeing Saul, he ran about hither and thither without hearth and home. See Aben Ezra and Kimchi. So the Chaldee here has אטלטלת, I have wandered about. Quite foreign will seem the version of the Arabic of Savary, Like a locust, انتقضت [intaqaḍtu], I am consumed. But with one dot fewer it should be read انتفضت [intafaḍtu], I am shaken off, as in the Paris edition, and in the Syriac ܐܬܢܦܨܬ, which is the same verb. In the Arabic MS. in my possession one reads قفزت [qafaztu], I leapt like a locust. This, though proper to the locust, does not suit this passage. [col. 458] But how wandering this animal is, how νομαδικὸν [nomadikon], and of uncertain abode, is nowhere taught so plainly as in Nahum ch. 3. There, after the Prophet has said to the city of Nineveh by way of concession (συγχωρητικῶς [synchōrētikōs]) in verses 15 and 16, Be as abundant as the bruchus, as numerous as the locusts, so that you multiply your merchants like the stars of heaven, he immediately adds by way of correction (κατ᾽ ἐπανόρθωσιν [kat᾽ epanorthōsin]), alluding to what he had said of the bruchus and the locusts: The bruchus, he says, has ravaged and flown away. Your princes shall be like locusts, and your captains כגוב גובי, like locusts; locusts, I say, which encamp in the hedges on a cold day; but when the sun rises they flee, and their place, where they were, is not known. As if he said: “You are indeed a most populous city, and your inhabitants seem to you equal in number to locusts. And within your walls many merchants and princes seek asylum, as locusts do in the hedges when they are cold. But there is no reason for you to trust in so numerous a multitude or in the wealth of these merchants, or to swell with pride at the strength of your princes and captains. For just as, when the sun rises, the locusts fly away and [III, 277] abandon the hedge that had been their refuge in the time of cold, so the peoples, merchants and princes who, when circumstances required, had fled to your walls, as soon as an occasion and hope of doing better elsewhere shines forth, will with one accord so abandon you that not even the least trace of them will remain.” Further, the Arabs elegantly express the flying away of locusts at sunrise by the verb اصقعر [iṣqaʿarra] ascaara. Alcamus: اصقعر الجراد اصابته الشمس وذهب [iṣqaʿarra al-jarād aṣābat-hu al-shams wa-dhahaba] Ascaara algirado, the sun struck the locusts and they went away. R. Selomo explains the words at the end of verse 15, התכבד כילק התכבדי כארבה, may you perish by sweeping away, as by the sweeping away of the bruchus and the locust. For these little creatures are wont to sweep everything away down to the dust, that is, to gnaw and scrape away everything in meadows, gardens and fields. Hence the Arabic name of the locust, جراد [jarād] girad, because the verb جرد [jarada] giarada, said of a field, means to make bare and to strip. But the verb התכבד in the sense of sweeping out occurs only among the Talmudists. Therefore others better refer it to abundance, which in Hebrew is כבד. And thus it coheres more fittingly with what follows, You have multiplied your merchants like the stars of heaven. What of the fact that in Exod. X, 14. we read of the locusts, And the locust went up over all the land of Egypt, and settled in all the territory of the Egyptians, כבד מאד, very heavy, namely in its abundance? Thus it is evident that this very כבד pertains to the size of the multitude, and consequently so does the verb התכבד derived from it.
